idiom_name: function* yielding values, consumed by for...of / spread / next()
implementation_notes: function* creates a generator function: calling it returns a Generator object that implements the iterator protocol (next()/return()/throw() with {value, done} results) and pauses at each yield with its whole execution context preserved; for...of, spread and Array.from drive it, and the consumer's break calls the generator's return() so finally blocks run. A value passed to next(v) becomes the result of the suspended yield expression, which is what makes generators work as pull-driven protocols; the async form (variant) adds await inside the body.
pitfalls: A generator object is single-shot: once done it returns {value: undefined, done: true} forever, so re-using the object silently yields nothing - call the generator function again for a fresh sequence.

Cleanup runs only when the generator is closed: abandoning a for...of or breaking out without the runtime calling return() (for example when the loop body throws and the error is caught outside) leaves finally blocks pending until the generator is collected.

Values sent with next(v) are ignored before the first yield (the first next() starts the body), and yield is an expression: a generator whose protocol is documented as push must handle unexpected input at the yield site.

variants.name: Async generators (async function*, for await...of)
variants.idiom_name: async function* with await inside, consumed by for await...of
variants.implementation_notes: async function* allows await inside the body and returns an AsyncGenerator whose next() resolves to {value, done}; for await...of drives it and yield* delegates to other async iterables. Use it when each element depends on an awaited source (fetch, timers, streams) and the consumer should apply backpressure by awaiting each pull; the loop's break/return closes the generator, and calling return() on the AsyncGenerator releases the producer - which must itself be awaited to run its finally blocks.
pitfalls: Closing an async generator is asynchronous: break/return triggers the generator's return(), which must be awaited (or the loop must be abandoned only when the runtime can run it) to release the underlying fetch or stream; a plain synchronous finally cannot await cleanup.

Rejections inside the body propagate through the consumer's loop, while floating promises started inside the body bypass the generator's error channel entirely; also, an AsyncGenerator cannot be consumed twice concurrently.
